newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street shares seen opening lower, await data.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street shares seen opening lower, await data.

text.p: U.S. stocks are expected to open slightly lower Wednesday, but much will hinge on keenly awaited inflation data due before the bell, analysts said.
"It all depends on what goes on at 8:30 a.m.," an analyst said, referring to the release at that time (1230 GMT) of July retail sales data and producer prices.
Analysts forecast a retail sales rise of 0.7 percent, compared with an increase of 0.5 percent in June.

Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, said the fear factor was increasing against a background of the UPS strike, concerns over higher interest rates, and reports of bidding wars in the housing market.
"If we get a stronger than expected retail sales figure, say over one percent, that would send long-term rates higher," Cardillo said.

On Tuesday U.S. blue chips staggered to their lowest close in three weeks after new evidence that U.S. economic growth is accelerating from its tame second quarter pace, raising the specter of interest rate hikes.

On Tuesday the Dow Industrials tumbled 101 points to close at 7961, its lowest finish since July 21. Nearly all of the decline followed the afternoon release of the Redbook retail sales index, which showed that retail sales rose a seasonally adjusted 0.9 percent in the week ended August 9.
The market will also be looking to see if an after-hours rally in shares of Applied Materials Inc will help boost the tech sector.
Applied Materials posted better than expected third quarter results.
The dollar fell overnight against the yen as long holders dumped their positions in line with the dollar/mark's fall, dealers said. The dollar was trading at 116.20.32 yen.
In Europe the dollar was dragged lower by an inflation warning in a Bundesbank report that boosted the mark to 1.8442/52.
Japan's Nikkei 225 index closed down 90.51 points, or 0.47 percent, at 19,008.60. In London the FTSE 100 was off 66.0 points at 5009.8.
U.S. stocks in London were mixed to weaker.

The Wall Street Journal said in its "Heard on the Street" column that a stealth rally was under way among embattled gold stocks, in part because of mounting investor worry about the future of the broader market.

The New York Times, in its "Marketplace" column, outlines the legal battle between Republic Industries Inc and two Japanese auto makers. Republic's stock has lost nearly half of its value since late January.
